question: A 35-year-old pedestrian is struck by a car and brought in with BP 80/50 mmHg, HR 130/min. Pelvic X-ray shows bilateral pubic rami fractures with widening of the symphysis pubis and both sacroiliac joints. Which Young-Burgess pattern does this represent, and what is the immediate pelvic intervention?

answers.text: Lateral Compression type II (LC-II) — apply pelvic binder over iliac crests

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: LC-II involves ipsilateral crescent fracture of the sacrum and contralateral open-book; it does not typically show bilateral SI joint widening, and the binder goes over the greater trochanters, not the iliac crests.

answers.text: Anteroposterior Compression type III (APC-III) — apply pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: APC-III = complete disruption of both anterior and posterior pelvic ligaments, resulting in the 'open-book' pelvis with bilateral SI widening. A binder (or sheet) applied at the greater trochanters is the first-line temporising measure to reduce pelvic volume and tamponade venous haemorrhage.

answers.text: Vertical Shear (VS) — immediate external fixator application in the emergency department

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: VS injuries are characterised by superior displacement (Malgaigne), not by bilateral SI widening alone. External fixation is part of definitive stabilisation, not the first ED step — a binder or pelvic C-clamp comes first for haemodynamic instability.

answers.text: Lateral Compression type I (LC-I) — no pelvic stabilisation required

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: LC-I (sacral buckle fracture + ipsilateral pubic rami fractures) reduces pelvic volume and is usually haemodynamically stable; bilateral SI widening is not a feature. Withholding binder in a haemodynamically unstable patient would be dangerous.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the Young-Burgess classification: AP-compression injuries cause progressive 'opening' of the pelvic ring (APC I→II→III) while lateral-compression injuries may actually reduce volume. Management keys on which ligaments are disrupted.

Correct. APC-III open-book injuries disrupt both anterior and posterior stabilisers, massively expanding pelvic volume. Immediate circumferential compression at the trochanters is the single most important first step before resuscitation, angioembolisation, or REBOA.
